title: UK SECR Guide (2026) for Apparel and Footwear
summary: SECR compliance explained for fashion brands: the 6 SECR reporting requirements, deadlines, and real brand examples.
body_markdown:
> Status: ✅ Approved law


If your brand has a large company registered in the UK, it most likely already reports carbon emissions every year. That obligation comes from SECR – Streamlined Energy and Carbon Reporting.


SECR reporting requirements (Scope 1 and 2 emissions) are light compared to


[frameworks like CSRD](https://www.carbonfact.com/blog/csrd-textile) . Yet, on average, SECR


[takes about 94 hours of staff time](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6a0dbf75faac4bc0b0e906af/2026-streamlined-energy-and-carbon-reporting-post-implementation-review.pdf) and costs about £7,100 a year. It is also often a brand's first public carbon disclosure, and the baseline everything else builds on.


That baseline matters increasingly in 2026. The UK Sustainability Reporting Standards (UK SRS), which include Scope 3 alongside Scope 1 and 2, become mandatory for listed companies from 2027. The UK is moving towards


[full GHG reporting](https://www.carbonfact.com/blog/knowledge/carbon-accounting-guide) .


Let’s break down what SECR compliance means for apparel and footwear companies today, with real examples from brands' own filings!


#### TL;DR


- **What:** SECR requires large UK companies to report their energy use, Scope 1 and 2 emissions, an intensity ratio, and energy efficiency actions in their annual report.


- **Who:** UK quoted companies, plus large UK companies and LLPs that meet 2 of 3 thresholds: £36m+ turnover, £18m+ balance sheet, 250+ employees. This includes the UK subsidiaries of non-UK brands.


- **When:** Every year, in the annual report. The deadline is 9 months after year-end for private companies and 6 months for public companies.


## What Is SECR?


SECR (Streamlined Energy and Carbon Reporting) is a UK regulation that requires large companies to publish their energy use and carbon emissions every year in their annual report. It has applied to every financial year starting on or after April 2019.


For most fashion brands, SECR covers the energy used by stores, offices, warehouses, and company vehicles. It does not cover products, materials, or manufacturing. Those sit in Scope 3, which is currently voluntary under SECR.


*Read our carbon*[accounting guide for apparel and footwear](https://www.carbonfact.com/blog/knowledge/carbon-accounting-guide) .


Source:[Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Accounting and Reporting Standard](https://ghgprotocol.org/sites/default/files/standards/Corporate-Value-Chain-Accounting-Reporing-Standard_041613_2.pdf) , page *5.*


## Key SECR Terms


-


Quoted company:


a UK company whose shares trade on the London Stock Exchange main market, an EEA regulated market, NYSE or Nasdaq.


-


Unquoted company:


any other company, including private companies and those on AIM (the London Stock Exchange’s market for smaller companies).


-


LLP (limited liability partnership):


a partnership whose members have limited liability, common for law and accounting firms but rare in fashion.


-


Annual report:


the yearly financial report every UK company must file. SECR figures go in its Directors’ Report section.


-


Companies House:


the UK government office that keeps company records. Filed annual reports are public there.


## Which Apparel and Footwear Brands Must Comply With SECR?


Three types of UK-registered entities must report:


1. Quoted companies:


UK companies whose shares are listed on the London Stock Exchange main market, an EEA regulated market, NYSE or Nasdaq. They must report regardless of their size.


*Examples:* Next, JD Sports Fashion.


2. Large unquoted companies:


Companies that meet at least 2 of these 3 requirements:


- turnover of £36m or more


- balance sheet total of £18m or more


- 250 or more employees


*Examples:* White Stuff Limited, Seasalt Limited


3. Large limited liability partnerships (LLPs):


Partnerships that meet the same 2 of 3 requirements. Few apparel or footwear brands are set up as LLPs.


### Do Non-UK Brands Have to Comply?


SECR does not apply to companies registered outside the UK, including foreign parent companies. But a UK-registered subsidiary must report if it meets the thresholds.


So a US, French, German, or Spanish brand with a large UK subsidiary is in scope. Examples from fashion brands that already reported:


- H&M (Sweden): H&M Hennes & Mauritz UK Limited


- Zara / Inditex (Spain): ITX UK Limited


- Levi's (US): Levi Strauss (U.K.) Limited


- Puma (Germany): PUMA United Kingdom Ltd


- Lacoste (France): Lacoste UK Limited


### What Are the SECR Exemptions?


-


Low energy use:


Brands using 40 MWh or less in the year don’t need to report their energy use or emissions, but must state in their report that they qualify for this exemption. In practice, this is very unlikely for fashion brands with stores, offices or warehouses.


-


Group report:


A large subsidiary does not need its own SECR report if its UK parent company's group report covers it.


*Example:* Clarks reports through its parent, C&J Clark (No 1) Limited. Kurt Geiger and Fat Face also report through their parent companies.


## SECR Reporting Requirements: 6 Things to Disclose


In-scope brands have 6 SECR reporting requirements:


1. Energy Use (kWh)


Energy use covers only the energy a brand uses itself: fuel burned in its own sites and vehicles (Scope 1) and the electricity it buys (Scope 2). Energy used in the supply chain, such as in fabric mills or factories (Scope 3), is not included.


Does it differ by company type? Yes.


- Quoted companies report total energy use worldwide, with the UK share shown separately.


- Large unquoted companies and LLPs report UK energy only, from gas, electricity and transport fuel.


2. Greenhouse Gas Emissions (tCO₂e)


Does it differ by company type? Yes.


- Quoted companies report Scope 1 and 2 emissions worldwide, with the UK share shown separately. This covers all fuel they burn, and the electricity, heat, steam and cooling they buy.


- Large unquoted companies and LLPs report UK emissions from gas, electricity and transport fuel. This includes fuel for business trips in employees’ own or hired cars. Bought heat, steam and cooling are optional.


**** **Quoted companies** **Large unquoted companies and LLPs**


Where Worldwide, with the UK share shown separately UK only


Scope 1 All fuel burned and emissions from running their sites Gas and transport fuel only


Scope 2 Bought electricity, heat, steam and cooling Bought electricity only


Business travel in employees' own or hired cars Not specifically required Required


3. At Least 1 Intensity Ratio


Does it differ by company type? No.


Every brand must show at least one intensity ratio – emissions compared to a business measure. This allows readers to compare years even when the business grows or shrinks. The brand picks the measure.


*Fashion examples:*


- Zara UK: tCO₂e per £m of turnover


- H&M UK: tCO₂e per square meter of retail space


- Puma UK: tCO₂e per square meter of floor space


- Boden: tCO₂e per employee


- Clarks: tCO₂e per £1,000 of turnover, and per 1,000 units sold


4. Methodology


Does it differ by company type? No.


Every brand must state how it calculated its figures. The law does not prescribe a method. The government recommends a recognized standard such as the


[GHG Protocol](https://www.carbonfact.com/blog/knowledge/carbon-accounting-guide)


Corporate Standard or ISO 14064-1. Most brands also use the UK Government's annual GHG conversion factors, which turn energy use (kWh) into emissions (tCO₂e).


*Fashion examples:*


- Levi's UK follows the GHG Protocol and reports emissions two ways: location-based and market-based. The market-based figure reflects its renewable electricity contracts.


- Seasalt follows the GHG Protocol and the government guidance, using an operational control boundary.


5. Energy Efficiency Actions


Does it differ by company type? No.


Every brand must describe, in words, the main actions it took to cut energy use that year. If it took none, it must say so.


*Fashion examples:*


- H&M UK fitted full LED lighting in 23 stores, upgraded track lighting in 17 stores and improved energy management systems in 13 stores.


- Lacoste UK sest timers to switch off window-display lighting and turns off IT equipment overnight.


6. Previous Year's Figures


Does it differ by company type? No.


Every brand must show last year's figures next to this year's, except in its first reporting year.


**Requirement** **Quoted companies** **Large unquoted companies and LLPs**


Energy use (kWh) Worldwide, UK share shown UK only: gas, electricity, transport fuel


Emissions (tCO₂e) Scope 1 and 2 worldwide, UK share shown UK only: gas, electricity, transport fuel, incl. business trips in employees' cars


Intensity ratio At least 1 At least 1


Methodology Required Required


Energy efficiency actions Required Required


Previous year's figures Required Required


Scope 3 Voluntary Voluntary


*(Overview of the SECR requirements)*


## How and Where Do Fashion Brands Report SECR?


SECR figures go in the brand's annual report, the yearly financial report every UK company must publish. The annual report is filed at Companies House, the UK government office that keeps company records. Once filed, it is public, so


[anyone can look up a brand's SECR figures](https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/) online.


NOTE:


A separate GHG or sustainability report does not replace this. Brands can reuse the same data, but the figures must appear in the annual report.

### What Happens If a Brand Doesn't Comply?


SECR is part of UK company law. Directors who fail to include compliant SECR figures in the annual report can face a fine, with no fixed upper limit set in law. The Financial Reporting Council (FRC) can also ask a court to order a corrected report.


Separately, late annual reports trigger automatic late filing penalties: £150 to £1,500 for private companies and £750 to £7,500 for PLCs, doubled if accounts are late 2 years in a row.


## Is UK SRS Replacing SECR?


The UK Sustainability Reporting Standards (UK SRS S1 and S2) are the UK version of the international ISSB standards. Published in February 2026, they will become mandatory for listed companies from 2027, on a “comply or explain” basis: brands either report the required information or publicly explain why they haven’t.


UK SRS does not replace SECR. The two rules apply side by side.


UK SRS goes much further than SECR. Brands report on climate risks, strategy, targets and Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions, measured with the GHG Protocol. Scope 3 applies from the second reporting year.


For fashion brands, this will mean covering materials, manufacturing and transport, which is where most of the footprint sits.


*Explore*[our textile regulations navigator by region](https://www.carbonfact.com/textile-regulations-hub?region=.all&status=.all&type=.all) *.*


## Learnings for Fashion Brands From the 2026 SECR Review


In May 2026, the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) published its


[post-implementation review of SECR](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/2026-post-implementation-review-of-the-secr-regulations-2018) , based on an independent evaluation. Here is what matters for fashion brands:


-


SECR costs more than expected.


Compliance takes about 94 hours of staff time and £7,100 a year on average, including outside help. Companies with 1,000+ employees spend about £12,200. 65% of ongoing costs go to consultants and auditors.


-


Avoid a UK-only baseline you will have to redo.


The review warns SECR's narrow scope can create "incomplete or UK-only baselines". When brands later add Scope 3 or other countries, emissions can appear to jump. Measure the full footprint from the start and report the SECR subset from it.


-


Numbers differ across reports.


Different rules can produce "multiple reported numbers for the same year". Use one dataset for SECR,


[CSRD](https://www.carbonfact.com/blog/csrd-textile) ,


[SB 253](https://www.carbonfact.com/blog/policy/californias-climate-laws)


and UK SRS.


-


Go beyond the minimum.


Investors want targets and transition plans. Companies with forward-looking commitments were more likely to report actual reductions.
